description: Fan of Princess Iron Fan: one wave puts out the fire, a second brings wind, a third brings rain; it can blow a man fifty thousand li (Journey to the West ch. 59–61).
Treasure cassock from the Buddha that Guanyin gives Tang Sanzang; stolen by the Black Bear Spirit and recovered by Sun Wukong (Journey to the West ch. 8, 12, 16–17).
Stones that Nüwa refines to repair the sky in both the Huainanzi Lan Ming and Liezi Tang Wen witnesses; glyph variants of the refining verb occur across received editions.
Gold band given by the Buddha to Guanyin and placed on Sun Wukong's head; Tang Sanzang's Tight-Fillet Spell makes it tighten (Journey to the West ch. 8, 14).

Harp made by Väinämöinen from the jawbone of a giant pike, its pegs from the pike's teeth and its strings from the hair of Hiisi's gelding; its music moves all creatures to tears, and it is lost overboard in Louhi's storm (Kalevala, Runes XL–XLIV).

Wonder-mill with a many-coloured lid forged by Ilmarinen from a swan's feather tip, a barren cow's milk, a barley grain and a summer ewe's wool; it grinds grain for eating, selling and storing, is locked in Pohjola's mountain, stolen and shattered at sea (Kalevala, Runes X, XXXIX–XLIII).
The ship of the Argonauts, built by Argus under Athena's direction, with a speaking beam of Dodonian oak (Argonautica 1, 4).
Fleece of the golden ram that carried Phrixus to Colchis, hung in the grove of Ares and guarded by a sleepless serpent (Argonautica 2, 4).
Nectar of immortality sought through the churning in both registered textual witnesses.
One of the four treasures of the Túatha Dé Danann in Cath Maige Tuired §6: brought from Murias, no company ever left it unsatisfied.
Pair of jewels given by the sea deity to Hoori: one makes the tide flow in to drown his brother, the other makes it ebb to save him (Kojiki, Sect. XL–XLI).
Ring of the dwarf Andvari, cursed by him to bring death to its owners; taken by Loki, passed through Fáfnir to Sigurðr and Brynhildr (Völsunga saga 14, 24, 27–28).
Heimdallr's horn, whose blast is heard in all worlds (Gylfaginning 27).
Ship made of dead men's nails that is loosed at Ragnarök and steered by the giant Hrymr (Gylfaginning 51).
Ship made by the sons of Ívaldi and given by Loki to Freyr; it has a fair wind as soon as its sail is hoisted and can be folded like a cloth and kept in a pocket (Skáldskaparmál 35; Gylfaginning 43).

尼奥尔德之子，掌管雨水、阳光与丰收；为娶葛德而交出宝剑（《欺骗古鲁菲》第24、37章）。 / Son of Njörðr who rules rain, sunshine and the fruitfulness of the earth; gives away his sword to win Gerðr (Gylfaginning 24, 37).
奥丁之妻，知晓一切命运；她让万物发誓不伤害巴德尔，唯独漏掉了槲寄生（《欺骗古鲁菲》第20、49章）。 / Odin's wife who knows all fates; she takes oaths from all things to protect Baldr, except the mistletoe (Gylfaginning 20, 49).

Blind god who, guided by Loki, throws the mistletoe that kills Baldr (Gylfaginning 49).

name_zh: 美狄亚恢复埃厄忒斯王位

description: 《荷马颂歌·致得墨忒耳》所叙珀耳塞福涅被哈得斯劫往冥界、得墨忒耳寻找女儿的事件层。 / Hymnic event layer for Persephone’s abduction and Demeter’s search.
Odysseus's ten-year wandering after Troy and his return to Ithaca to defeat the suitors, as told in the Odyssey's twenty-four books.

canonical_name: From Chaos to the reign of Zeus (Theogony)
description: Hesiod's account of the first beings, the overthrow of Ouranos and Cronus, the war with the Titans, Typhoeus and the reign of Zeus.
name_zh: 从卡俄斯到宙斯为王（《神谱》）

description: Combat narrated in Hesiod Theogony 820-868.
NPS summary of Hawaiian oral history: Pele voyages from Kahiki, moves southeast through the islands and settles in Halemaʻumaʻu.
name_zh: 佩蕾从卡希基出发的旅程

description: Textual narrative event registered from separate Mahābhārata critical-edition and Bhāgavata Purāṇa witnesses; kept distinct from the Angkor Wat material-witness scene.
From Rāma's exile and Rāvaṇa's abduction of Sītā to the bridge to Laṅkā, the war and Rāma's coronation (Books II–VI).
name_zh: 悉多被劫与救回（《罗摩衍那》）

description: Battle between the Túatha Dé Danann and the Fomoire in Cath Maige Tuired, in which Lug kills Balor.
name_zh: 第二次马格图雷德之战

canonical_name: Amaterasu hides in the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling
description: Amaterasu shuts herself in the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling after Susanoo's ravages; the deities' assembly, mirror, jewels and Ame-no-Uzume's dance bring her out (Kojiki, Sect. XV–XVI).
name_zh: 天之岩户：天照大神隐入岩屋

description: Izanagi washes after returning from Yomi; deities are born from his washing, ending with Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi and Susanoo.
After Izanami's death Izanagi follows her to the land of the dead and asks her to return.
A source-scoped living shrine account linked to Yamato Takeru; it does not prove uninterrupted physical custody.

canonical_name: Discovery of Kusanagi in Yamata no Orochi
description: Academic-reference-scoped event connecting Susanoo, Yamata no Orochi and Kusanagi.
name_zh: 从八岐大蛇体内发现草薙剑

description: Izanagi and Izanami stir the brine with the heavenly jewelled spear from the Floating Bridge of Heaven.

canonical_name: Churning of the Sea of Milk scene at Angkor Wat
description: The scene as represented by the Angkor Wat relief; it is not treated as a complete Sanskrit textual version.
name_zh: 吴哥寺乳海搅拌图像事件

canonical_name: Hero Twins and Seven Macaw episode
description: A bounded episode indexed from a public K'iche'-attributed Smithsonian overview, not a universal Maya master narrative.
name_zh: 英雄双子与七金刚鹦鹉事件

description: Common thread named by Te Ara: the children of Ranginui and Papatūānuku separate their parents, letting light into the world.
name_zh: 兰吉努伊与帕帕图阿努库的分离

description: Florentine Codex Book 3, chapter 1: Huitzilopochtli is born fully armed and defeats Coyolxauhqui and the Centzon Huitznahua.
name_zh: 维齐洛波奇特利诞生于蛇山

canonical_name: End of Quetzalcoatl's glory at Tollan
description: Florentine Codex Book 3, chapters 3–14: sorcerers including Titlacauan come to Quetzalcoatl and his glory at Tollan ends.
The Æsir bind the wolf Fenrir; Týr's hand is bitten off (Gylfaginning 34).
Baldr is killed despite Frigg's oaths (Gylfaginning 49).
Smithing contest that produces Gullinbursti, Draupnir and Mjölnir.
historical_period: Mythic narrative preserved in medieval text

canonical_name: Slaying of Ymir and the shaping of the world
description: Odin and his brothers kill the primordial giant Ymir and make the world from his body (Gylfaginning 7–8).
name_zh: 尤弥尔被杀与世界成形

description: Thor, Loki and Þjálfi travel to Útgarðr, lose every contest to illusions, and learn the truth as they leave (Gylfaginning 44–47).
name_zh: 索尔前往乌特加尔洛基之城

canonical_name: Reconstructed Transfer of the Darius Statue to Susa
description: 学术资料重建的历史转运事件；不是现存古代叙事原文，也不把“由薛西斯带到苏萨”升级为无争议事实。 / Scholarly reconstruction of the statue transfer, not an extant ancient narrative and not treated as undisputed fact.
historical_period: Attributed to the reign of Xerxes I, after 486 BCE
name_zh: 大流士雕像转运苏萨（学术重建）

canonical_name: The Kyiv idols are cast down (988)
description: Primary Chronicle annal 988: after his baptism Volodimer orders the idols overthrown; Perun is dragged down the hill and thrown into the Dnieper.

canonical_name: Volodimer's idols on the Kyiv hill (980)
description: Primary Chronicle annal 980: Volodimer sets up idols of Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl and Mokosh on the hill outside the palace hall.
In ETCSL 1.1.1 Enki eats the plants, Ninhursaĝa curses him, and later she brings forth deities to heal his ailing body.
name_zh: 恩基的病与宁胡尔萨格的救治

description: Gilgameš sets out for the mountains; Utu is asked for help and grants guides.
name_zh: 吉尔伽美什远征胡瓦瓦

description: The moon god travels by boat with gifts to his father Enlil's city Nibru and returns with blessings for Urim.
name_zh: 南纳前往尼普尔的旅程

canonical_name: Baal and Mot sequence in KTU 1.5–1.6
description: 把争执、死亡／冥界与返回阶段登记为残缺文本序列，不简化为“巴力永久杀死死亡”。 / Fragmentary narrative sequence, not a timeless claim that Death was permanently destroyed.
historical_period: Late Bronze Age narrative witnessed by KTU 1.5–1.6

canonical_name: Baal and Yamm in KTU 1.2 IV
description: 限定于 KTU 1.2 IV 的神话战斗层。 / Witness-specific mythic combat layer for KTU 1.2 IV.
historical_period: Late Bronze Age Ugaritic textual witness

description: 严格限定于《梨俱吠陀》1.32 的神话叙事事件层。 / Witness-specific event layer for Rigveda 1.32.
name_zh: 因陀罗与弗栗多之战（《梨俱吠陀》1.32）

canonical_name: Creation of the sixteen lands and their counter-creations
description: Videvdad 1: Ahura Mazda makes sixteen good lands; each time Angra Mainyu counter-creates a plague.
name_zh: 十六地的创造与反创造

description: 卡纳克与卢克索之间的节庆与神像巡行传统；当前只保存官方遗址公开层。 / Theban festival and cult-image procession between Karnak and Luxor; current record is limited to public official-site evidence.
historical_period: New Kingdom and later Theban festival layers

description: 从雅典沿圣道前往厄琉息斯的公共节庆／行列层；不等同于秘仪内部全部活动。 / Public festival and procession layer from Athens along the Sacred Way, distinct from all inner initiatory acts.
historical_period: Classical and later public festival layers

description: 京都持续举行的公开节庆与仪式传统；神社所述起源、历史制度和现代行列分层保存。 / Continuing Kyoto festival whose shrine-origin narrative, historical institutions and modern procession remain layered.
historical_period: Living annual festival with layered historical tradition

description: 奥约社群每年举行的活态传统；公开层与仅限入门者内容严格分离。 / Annual Oyo living tradition with public and initiated-only knowledge boundaries kept separate.

Strongest of the giants, with a three-cornered heart of stone, a stone head, a stone shield and a whetstone for a weapon; after a horse race with Óðinn he boasts drunkenly in Ásgarðr and is slain by Thor at Grjótúnagarðar (Skáldskaparmál 17).
Clay giant nine leagues tall made by the giants at Grjótúnagarðar to stand beside Hrungnir, given a mare's heart that quailed when Thor came; felled by Thjálfi (Skáldskaparmál 17).
阿蒙、穆特、孔苏的底比斯神族组合；成员关系不取代每位神的独立档案。 / Cult grouping of Amun, Mut and Khonsu; membership does not merge the deities.
historical_period: New Kingdom and later cult organization

canonical_name: Eight Thunder Kami of the Kojiki
description: 伊邪那美身上的八位雷神群组；不自动等同于后世单一雷神人格。 / Group entity for the eight thunder kami on Izanami in the Kojiki Yomi episode.

Son of Gan Jiang and Mo Ye, 'a foot between the brows', who gives his own head and sword to a stranger to avenge his father on the king of Chu; the three heads are buried as the Tomb of the Three Kings (Soushen ji, juan 11).
Rebellious lord who, in the Shiji Annals of the Five Emperors, disobeys the ruler and is captured and killed by Xuanyuan at Zhuolu.
Filial son of the Han who sells himself to bury his father and is helped to repay the debt by a wife who proves to be the Weaving Maiden of heaven (Soushen ji, juan 1).
Swordsmith of Chu who takes three years to forge a pair of swords for the king, hides the male sword for his unborn son, and is killed by the angry king (Soushen ji, juan 11).
Youngest of six daughters of Li Dan of Jiangle, who volunteers as the sacrifice to the great serpent of Mount Yong and kills it with a sword, a dog and honeyed rice cakes (Soushen ji, juan 19).
Wife of Gan Jiang who keeps her husband's last words and tells their son where the hidden sword lies (Soushen ji, juan 11).
Former Curtain-Raising General banished to the Flowing Sands River for breaking a crystal cup; Tang Sanzang's third disciple in Journey to the West.
The immortal teacher in Journey to the West who names Sun Wukong and teaches him the seventy-two transformations and the somersault cloud.
《西游记》中石头里生出的美猴王：大闹天宫，后来成为唐三藏的大徒弟。 / The stone-born Monkey King of Journey to the West, who wreaks havoc in heaven and becomes Tang Sanzang's first disciple.
Immortal of the Golden Light Cave on Qianyuan Mountain in Investiture of the Gods; Nezha's teacher, who rebuilds his body from lotus.

The scripture pilgrim of Journey to the West, born Chen Jiangliu and reincarnated from the Buddha's disciple Golden Cicada; the novel's figure is kept separate from the historical monk Xuanzang (602–664).
《史记·五帝本纪》中少典之子轩辕，于涿鹿擒杀蚩尤并被尊为天子；本站不作历史真实性断言。 / Xuanyuan, son of Shaodian, who in the Shiji fights Chiyou at Zhuolu and is honoured as Son of Heaven; no historical-reality claim is made.
Former Marshal of the Heavenly Canopy, reborn with a pig's face after offending the moon goddess; Tang Sanzang's second disciple in Journey to the West.
Legendary sovereign named as the rival of Gonggong in the Huainanzi and Liezi witnesses; no historical-reality claim is made.
Youngest daughter of King Fuchai of Wu, who dies of grief when her father refuses Han Zhong, meets him as a ghost at her tomb, and appears to her father to clear him (Soushen ji, juan 16).

canonical_name: Anubis (elder brother in the Tale of Two Brothers)
description: Elder brother of Bata in the Tale of Two Brothers, a farmer who is deceived by his wife, later restores Bata to life and succeeds him as king; his name is the god's name Anubis, but in the tale he is a man (Papyrus D'Orbiney).
name_zh: 阿努比斯（两兄弟故事中的哥哥）

description: Younger brother in the Tale of Two Brothers, a herdsman with the strength of a god, who flees false accusation, places his heart on the flower of a pine, dies and is restored, and becomes king of Egypt (Papyrus D'Orbiney).
Sister of Joukahainen promised against her will to the old Väinämöinen; she drowns in the sea and, caught by him as a strange fish, slips back into the waves (Kalevala, Runes IV–V).
Eternal smith of Kalevala who forged the vault of the sky and forges the Sampo for the mistress of Pohjola to win her daughter (Kalevala, Runes X, XVIII–XXV, XXXVII–XLIII).

Young singer of the north who challenges Väinämöinen, is sung into a swamp and buys his life with the promise of his sister Aino; later he shoots Väinämöinen's horse from under him (Kalevala, Runes III, VI).

Son of Kalervo, born in captivity after his uncle Untamo destroys his kin; sold as a slave to Ilmarinen, he avenges the stone baked in his bread, unknowingly seduces his own sister, destroys Untamo's clan and dies on his own sword (Kalevala, Runes XXXI–XXXVI).
The flower of Saari, carried off by Lemminkäinen in his sledge; her broken vow not to go to the village dances sends him to Pohjola (Kalevala, Runes XI–XII).

Handsome, reckless hero of Kalevala, also called Ahti and Kaukomieli, who carries off Kyllikki, goes to Pohjola to woo, is killed at the river of Tuonela and restored by his mother (Kalevala, Runes XI–XV, XXVI–XXX, XXXIX–XLIII).
Mother who warns Lemminkäinen against Pohjola, reads his death in the bleeding brush, rakes his body from the river of Tuonela and restores him to life (Kalevala, Runes XII, XV).
Gap-toothed mistress of Pohjola, a powerful sorceress who demands the Sampo as the price of her daughter and pursues its thieves as a great eagle (Kalevala, Runes VII, X, XLII–XLIII and elsewhere).
Daughter of Louhi, seen weaving on the rainbow, who sets Väinämöinen impossible tasks and later marries Ilmarinen (Kalevala, Runes VIII, X, XVIII–XXV, XXXIII).

Ancient singer and sage of Kalevala, born old from Ilmatar after thirty summers in the womb; he sings Joukahainen into a swamp, seeks a bride in Pohjola, makes the first kantele and leads the theft of the Sampo (Kalevala, Runes I–L).
King of Argos, warned by an oracle that his daughter's son would kill him; killed by Perseus's discus at Larissa.
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Hunter, son of Aristaeus and Autonoe, raised by Chiron; changed into a deer by Artemis when he saw her bathing and devoured by his own fifty hounds on Cithaeron (Apollodorus, Library 3.4.4).
科尔喀斯神话国王、赫利俄斯之子；本批仅建立与同名审计直接有关的兄弟和王位叙事。 / Mythic king of Colchis and son of Helios; current scope is limited to the Perses identity audit.
Son of Aphrodite and Anchises, foretold in the Hymn to Aphrodite to be reared by the mountain nymphs of Ida and to rule among the Trojans (Homeric Hymn 5, lines 196–199, 256–280).
Granddaughter of Perseus and mother of Heracles by Zeus and of Iphicles by Amphitryon (Library 2.4.6–2.4.8).
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Grandson of Perseus, husband of Alcmena and foster-father of Heracles, exiled from Tiryns to Thebes (Library 2.4.6–2.4.11).
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Trojan prince who herds cattle on Mount Ida; Aphrodite, made by Zeus to desire him, comes to him disguised as a Phrygian princess and bears him Aeneas (Homeric Hymn 5).
本批仅建立希罗多德7.61所需的母系关系入口；其他版本继续扩张。 / Current baseline supports the Herodotean parentage claim; other narrative versions remain open.
historical_period: Archaic and Classical Greek heroic tradition

description: Son of Aeetes and brother of Medea, who pursues the Argonauts and is killed by Jason in an ambush (Argonautica 4).
Companion of Artemis in the chase, sworn to maidenhood; loved by Zeus, turned into a bear and shot down by Artemis, then set among the stars as the Bear (Apollodorus, Library 3.8.2).
Daughter of King Acrisius of Argos, shut in a bronze chamber and visited by Zeus as a shower of gold; mother of Perseus.
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Daughter of Oeneus of Calydon and wife of Heracles, won by his wrestling with Achelous; she unknowingly kills him with the robe smeared with Nessus's blood (Library 2.7.5–2.7.7).
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Son of Tydeus, lord of Argos and one of the foremost Achaean warriors at Troy; with Athena beside him he wounds Aphrodite and then Ares himself (Iliad 5).
King of Tiryns and Mycenae, born before Heracles through Hera's contrivance, who imposed the twelve labours (Library 2.4.5, 2.4.12–2.5.12).
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Trojan youth whom Zeus carried off for his beauty to pour wine for the gods; Zeus consoled his father Tros with immortal horses (Homeric Hymn 5, lines 202–217).
Son of Zeus and Alcmena, the greatest of Greek heroes, who performed the twelve labours for Eurystheus and after death on Mount Oeta was received among the gods (Library 2.4.8–2.7.7).
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Queen of the Amazons whose belt, given by Ares, Heracles fetched for Eurystheus's daughter (Library 2.5.9).
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Young companion of Heracles, drawn into a spring by a water-nymph in Mysia, so that Heracles is left behind (Argonautica 1).
Queen of Lemnos, whose women had killed their menfolk, who welcomes Jason and the Argonauts (Argonautica 1).
Son of Iphicles and nephew of Heracles, his charioteer against the Lernaean hydra (Library 2.5.2).
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Daughter of Eurytus of Oechalia, promised as an archery prize and refused to Heracles, later taken captive by him (Library 2.6.1, 2.7.7).
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Daughter of Agamemnon, brought to Aulis to be sacrificed to Artemis so the fleet could sail; the goddess snatched her away to the Taurians, put a deer in her place and made her priestess (Apollodorus, Epitome 3.21–22).
Son of Aeson and leader of the Argonauts, sent by King Pelias to fetch the golden fleece from Colchis, which he wins with Medea's help.
Aged father of Odysseus who lives in grief on his farm while the suitors occupy the palace, and fights beside his son and grandson at the Odyssey's close.
埃厄忒斯之女；《书库》叙事中杀死夺位的珀耳塞斯并恢复父亲王位。 / Daughter of Aeetes who in the Library kills the usurping Perses and restores her father.

Daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion of Thebes, who boasted she was more blessed in children than Leto; Artemis and Apollo shot her children, and she was turned to weeping stone on Sipylus (Apollodorus, Library 3.5.6).
King of Ithaca and hero of the Odyssey, who wanders ten years after the fall of Troy before returning home to defeat his wife's suitors.
Queen of Lydia, daughter of Iardanes, who bought Heracles as a slave when Hermes sold him in penance for the murder of Iphitus (Library 2.6.3).
historical_period: Greek heroic myth (Library, 1st–2nd century CE compilation)

description: Giant hunter, born of Earth or son of Poseidon, who could stride across the sea; carried off by Eos to Delos and slain by Artemis (Apollodorus, Library 1.4.3–1.4.5).
Thracian singer among the Argonauts, whose song calms quarrels and drowns out the Sirens (Argonautica 1, 4).
King of Iolcus, warned to beware the man with one sandal, who sends Jason on the quest for the golden fleece.
Wife of Odysseus, who keeps the suitors at bay for years with the trick of the unwoven shroud and tests her returned husband with the secret of their bed.
King of Thebes, son of Agave and Echion, who tried to stop the Bacchic rites; spying on the women on Cithaeron, he was torn apart by his own mother in her frenzy (Apollodorus, Library 3.5.2).
希罗多德7.61中的珀耳修斯与安德洛墨达之子，用于解释“波斯人”名称；不是两位同名神祇。 / Son of Perseus and Andromeda in Herodotus 7.61, used in a Persian-name aition; distinct from the homonymous gods.
name_zh: 珀耳塞斯（珀耳修斯之子）

description: 本批仅建立希罗多德7.61所需的父系关系入口；完整英雄事迹仍在队列扩张。 / Current baseline supports the Herodotean parentage claim; the broader heroic dossier remains queued.
historical_period: Archaic and Classical Greek heroic tradition

description: Blind seer of Thrace tormented by the Harpies, freed by the sons of Boreas, who foretells the Argonauts' route (Argonautica 2).
Son of Zeus and twin of Castor, the boxer among the Argonauts, who kills the Bebrycian king Amycus (Argonautica 2).
Son of Odysseus and Penelope, who sails in search of news of his father and fights beside him against the suitors.

Trojan beloved of Eos; she asked Zeus to make him immortal but forgot to ask for ageless youth, so he grew old for ever and she shut him in a chamber where his voice flows on endlessly (Homeric Hymn 5, lines 218–238; Theogony 984).
《得墨忒耳颂歌》与厄琉息斯图像中的英雄人物；不同传统版本继续分层。 / Hero attested in the Hymn to Demeter and Eleusinian imagery; variant traditions remain open.
Young son of Arjuna and Subhadrā who breaks into the Kaurava circular array on the thirteenth day but, not knowing the way out, is killed by many warriors together (Mahābhārata, Drona Parva).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Wife of the sage Gautama, cursed after Indra's deception and released when Rāma enters the hermitage.
Son of Droṇa who, after the war, raids the sleeping Pāṇḍava camp by night, kills Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Draupadī's sons, and is cursed by Kṛṣṇa (Mahābhārata, Drona and Sauptika Parvas).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Son of Kaikeyī who refuses the throne won for him and rules Ayodhyā in the name of Rāma's sandals.
Second of the Pāṇḍavas, son of Vāyu, of enormous strength, who vows vengeance for Draupadī's humiliation and breaks Duryodhana's thighs with his mace (Mahābhārata, passim).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Grandsire of the Kurus, son of Gaṅgā, bound by his vow of celibacy and his loyalty to the Kuru throne; first commander of the Kaurava army, he falls on the tenth day onto a bed of arrows and chooses the hour of his death (Mahābhārata, passim).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Princess of Vidarbha who chooses Nala at her svayaṃvara by recognising him among four gods in his likeness, survives abandonment in the forest and devises the second svayaṃvara that brings him back (Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Nalopākhyāna).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: King of Ayodhyā and father of Rāma, bound by two boons to Kaikeyī; he dies of grief after Rāma's exile.
Daughter of Drupada and wife of the five Pāṇḍavas, humiliated in the Kuru hall after the dice game, whose five sons are killed in Aśvatthāman's night raid (Mahābhārata, passim).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Brahmin teacher of arms to both Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas and second commander of the Kaurava army, who lays down his weapons on hearing that Aśvatthāman is dead and is slain by Dhṛṣṭadyumna (Mahābhārata, passim).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Eldest of the hundred Kaurava brothers, who wins the Pāṇḍavas' kingdom through the rigged dice game, refuses peace, and is struck down by Bhīma's mace at the end of the war (Mahābhārata, passim).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: King of Mithilā who found Sītā in a ploughed furrow and promised her to whoever could string the bow of Śiva.
Queen of Daśaratha and mother of Bharata, who uses two old boons to have Rāma exiled for fourteen years.

Son of Kuntī by the sun god, raised by a charioteer, friend of Duryodhana and rival of Arjuna, who kills Ghaṭotkaca with Indra's dart and is slain by Arjuna when his chariot wheel sinks (Mahābhārata, passim).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Rāma's younger half-brother and constant companion in exile, who slays Indrajit in the war at Laṅkā.

King of the Nishadhas, chosen by Damayantī over four gods; possessed by Kali, he loses his kingdom at dice, abandons his wife in the forest, serves King Ṛtuparṇa as the charioteer Bāhuka and regains wife and kingdom (Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Nalopākhyāna).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Axe-bearing brahmin warrior, destroyer of kṣatriyas, who challenges Rāma after the breaking of Śiva's bow and yields when Rāma strings the bow of Vishnu.

Son of the blind, exiled King Dyumatsena of Śālva, raised in a forest hermitage; foretold to die a year after his marriage to Sāvitrī, he is restored to life when Yama yields to her (Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Pativratā-māhātmya).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Daughter of King Aśvapati of Madra, born by the boon of the goddess Sāvitrī, who chooses the exiled prince Satyavān knowing he will die within a year, follows Yama when he takes Satyavān's life, and wins it back by her steadfastness and wisdom (Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Pativratā-māhātmya).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Vānara prince exiled by his brother Vālin, who allies with Rāma and becomes king of Kiṣkindhā.
Vānara king of Kiṣkindhā, son of Indra, who seized his brother Sugrīva's wife and is shot by Rāma from concealment.
Rāvaṇa's righteous younger brother, who counsels the return of Sītā, takes refuge with Rāma and is crowned king of Laṅkā.
King turned brahmin sage who takes the young Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to guard his sacrifice, gives Rāma the divine weapons and leads him to Mithilā.
Eldest of the five Pāṇḍavas, son of Dharma, who loses the kingdom at dice, endures exile, and in the war speaks the half-truth that brings down Droṇa (Mahābhārata, passim).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: King of Connacht and husband of Medb, whose bull Finnbennach makes his possessions greater than hers (Táin Bó Cúalnge).
King of Ulster at Emain Macha, uncle and foster-father of Cú Chulainn, who leads the Ulstermen when they rise from their debility (Táin Bó Cúalnge).
Foster-brother of Cú Chulainn, trained with him by Scáthach, who is persuaded by Medb to fight him at the ford and is killed on the fourth day (Táin Bó Cúalnge).
Queen of Connacht who musters the four provinces to carry off the Brown Bull of Cúailnge so that her wealth will equal her husband's (Táin Bó Cúalnge).
Woman of Owari whom Yamato Takeru promises to marry on his way east and weds on his return; he leaves the Kusanagi sword with her before going to Mount Ibuki (Kojiki, Sect. LXXXIII, LXXXVII).
Consort of Yamato Takeru who enters the sea at the Hashirimizu crossing to calm the waves sent by the deity of the strait; her comb washes ashore seven days later (Kojiki, Sect. LXXXIV).
Aunt of Yamato Takeru serving at the shrine of Ise, who lends him her robes for the Kumaso deed and gives him the Kusanagi sword and a bag holding a fire-striker (Kojiki, Sect. LXXX, LXXXII).
Wild man fashioned from clay by the goddess Aruru as Gilgamesh's equal; his friendship and death drive the Standard Babylonian epic.
Survivor of the Flood granted eternal life by the gods, who tells Gilgamesh the Flood story in Tablet XI.
Shield-maiden put to sleep by Odin's sleep-thorn for disobeying him, woken by Sigurðr, betrothed to him, and later deceived into marrying Gunnarr (Völsunga saga 20–32).
Daughter of King Gjúki, married to Sigurðr after her mother's potion makes him forget Brynhildr; her quarrel with Brynhildr leads to his death (Völsunga saga 25–31).
Son of Gjúki, who wins Brynhildr through Sigurðr riding the flames in his shape and later consents to Sigurðr's killing (Völsunga saga 26–32).
Son of Völsungr who alone draws Odin's sword from the Branstock, avenges his father, and dies when Odin breaks his sword; father of Sigurðr (Völsunga saga 3–12).
Daughter of Völsungr and twin of Sigmundr, married against her will to Siggeir, who bears Sinfjötli to her brother and dies in Siggeir's burning hall (Völsunga saga 3–8).
Son of Sigmundr and Hjördís, slayer of the dragon Fáfnir, who wakes Brynhildr and is killed through the Gjúkungs' oath-breaking (Völsunga saga 13–32).
Son of Sigmundr and his sister Signý, raised in the forest to avenge the Völsungs, poisoned by Borghildr and carried off by a mysterious ferryman (Völsunga saga 7–10).
Farmer's son who becomes Thor's servant after breaking the goat's thigh bone, and races Hugi at Útgarðr (Gylfaginning 44–46).
King of Hunland, great-grandson of Odin, born after six years in the womb, who built his hall round the oak Branstock and fell fighting Siggeir (Völsunga saga 2–5).
Warrior maiden of the White Castle who rides out in armour against Sohrāb, is unmasked when he knocks off her helmet, and escapes him by a promise and a jest from the walls (Shahnameh).
Greatest champion of the Shahnameh, son of Zāl and Rūdābeh, born by the Simorgh's counsel; he rides Rakhsh, passes the seven stages to free Kay Kāvus and unknowingly kills his son Sohrāb (Shahnameh).
Daughter of Mehrāb of Kābul, a descendant of Zahhāk, who loves Zāl, offers her hair as a rope to her tower, and gives birth to Rostam by a cut made on the Simorgh's counsel (Shahnameh).
Champion of King Manūchehr and lord of Zābulistān, who exposes his white-haired newborn son Zāl on Mount Alborz and, repenting after a dream, takes him back from the Simorgh (Shahnameh).

Son of Rostam and Tahmineh, raised in Samangān, who leads a Turanian army into Iran hoping to set his father on the throne, and is killed by Rostam, neither knowing the other until too late (Shahnameh).
Princess of Samangān who comes to Rostam by night, marries him and bears Sohrāb; she gives her son the token by which his father should know him and dies of grief after his death (Shahnameh).
Son of Sām, born with white hair, exposed and raised by the Simorgh on Mount Alborz; he wins Rūdābeh of Kābul against his father's and the king's objections and fathers Rostam (Shahnameh).
Lord of Unug (Uruk) in the Sumerian Gilgameš poems; kept separate from the later Akkadian epic's text entity.
name_zh: 吉尔伽美什（苏美尔语诗篇）

description: Daughter of Dôn who fails Math's test of maidenhood, bearing Dylan and Lleu, and lays three destinies on Lleu: no name, no arms and no human wife save from her (Fourth Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Giant king of the Island of the Mighty, son of Llŷr, who wades to Ireland to avenge his sister Branwen and whose severed head presides over the feast at Harlech and Gwales (Second Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)
name_zh: 本迪盖德弗兰（受福的布兰）

description: Woman made by Math and Gwydion from the flowers of oak, broom and meadowsweet as Lleu's wife, who plots his death with Gronw Pebr and is turned into an owl (Fourth Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Daughter of Llŷr, married to Matholwch of Ireland and humiliated there, who sends a starling to her brother and dies of grief that two islands were laid waste for her (Second Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Quarrelsome half-brother of Bendigeidfran who maims Matholwch's horses, throws Gwern into the fire and breaks the cauldron of rebirth at the cost of his life (Second Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Magician and storyteller, nephew of Math, who tricks Pryderi out of his swine, raises Lleu, outwits Arianrhod's curses and turns Blodeuedd into an owl (Fourth Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Son of Arianrhod, named 'the fair one with the skilful hand', armed and married through Gwydion's craft, who survives Blodeuedd's betrayal as an eagle (Fourth Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Son of Llŷr, brother of Bendigeidfran, one of the seven survivors of the war in Ireland, who marries Rhiannon and lifts the enchantment on Dyfed (Second and Third Branches).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Magician-king of Gwynedd who must keep his feet in a maiden's lap except in war, punishes his nephews by turning them into beasts, and with Gwydion makes Blodeuedd from flowers (Fourth Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: King of Ireland who marries Branwen and, insulted by Efnysien's maiming of his horses, receives the cauldron of rebirth in amends (Second Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Son of Pwyll and Rhiannon, stolen at birth and raised by Teyrnon as Gwri Golden-hair, later lord of Dyfed, killed by Gwydion (First to Fourth Branches).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Prince of Dyfed who changes places with Arawn, king of Annwn, for a year, wins Rhiannon and is called Head of Annwn (First Branch).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: Lady of the Otherworld on a white horse who chooses Pwyll, is falsely accused of killing her son, and later marries Manawydan (First and Third Branches).
historical_period: Four Branches of the Mabinogi (Middle Welsh, c. 11th–12th century)

description: 阿契美尼德国王；本批只建立苏萨雕像与埃及神学语境的有来源连接。 / Achaemenid king, here limited to the sourced Susa-statue and Egyptian-theological context.
阿契美尼德国王；本批仅登记其完成苏萨王宫工程及被学界归因的大流士雕像转运。 / Achaemenid king, limited here to sourced Susa building completion and the attributed statue transfer.
Second Tang emperor (r. 626–649). Journey to the West portrays him visiting the underworld and sending Tang Sanzang west; those episodes belong to the novel, not to history.
Great Royal Wife of Thutmose I and mother of Hatshepsut; in the Deir el-Bahari birth cycle Amun-Re comes to her in the form of her husband and she bears the divine child.

Eighteenth-Dynasty queen who ruled Egypt as king (c. 1479–1458 BCE), named Maatkare; the birth cycle in her temple at Deir el-Bahari presents her as the daughter of Amun-Re, conceived when the god visited Queen Ahmose.
Nineteenth-Dynasty king of Egypt (reigned c. 1279–1213 BCE), named Usermaatre-Setepenre; the Bentresh Stela, composed centuries later, sets its tale of Khonsu's healing journey in his reign.

Kushite king of Egypt of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty (late 8th century BCE) who had the Memphite Theology copied onto a stone slab in the temple of Ptah at Memphis, saying the old original was worm-eaten.
Eighteenth-Dynasty king, husband of Ahmose and father of Hatshepsut, whose form Amun-Re takes in the Deir el-Bahari birth cycle.
江户时代艺术家；本批仅登记其有馆藏证据的风神雷神屏风摹本。 / Edo-period artist, scoped here to the museum-documented Wind and Thunder God screens.
江户时代艺术家；宗达与光琳作品接受史中的独立人物。 / Edo-period artist in the reception history of Sōtatsu and Kōrin.
京都国立博物馆归属《风神雷神图屏风》的画家；历史人物与神话实体分开。 / Historical painter to whom Kyoto National Museum attributes the screens.
historical_period: Edo period, active early seventeenth century

description: 当前展示苏萨大流士雕像的现代博物馆机构；未核实的馆藏号不写入。 / Modern institution displaying the Darius statue; no unverified inventory number is asserted.
为宗达《风神雷神图屏风》提供官方目录与展示记录的现代机构。 / Modern institution providing the official catalogue and exhibition record for the Sotatsu screens.
保存光琳《风神雷神图屏风》等日本文化财产的现代机构。 / Modern museum holding Kōrin’s Wind and Thunder God screens.
收藏大厄琉息斯浮雕126号的现代博物馆机构。 / Modern holding institution for the Great Eleusinian Relief no. 126.
保存和公开研究喜马拉雅艺术对象的现代机构。 / Modern institution holding Himalayan art objects.
name_zh: 鲁宾喜马拉雅艺术博物馆

description: 现代影视角色版本；在该连续性中为索尔的同父异母姐姐。 / Modern screen-continuity interpretation in which Hela is Thor’s half-sister.
现代影视角色版本；在该连续性中为索尔的养兄弟。 / Modern screen-continuity interpretation in which Loki is Thor’s adoptive brother.
现代影视角色版本；与古诺斯索尔分离。 / Modern screen-continuity interpretation, separate from the Old Norse entity.

canonical_name: Wind and Thunder God Screens attributed to Sakai Hōitsu — research record
description: 京都国立博物馆仅确认抱一亦作过版本；馆藏、编号与精确年代未核实前不补写。 / Research record for the Hōitsu version noted by Kyoto National Museum; custody, catalogue and exact date remain unasserted.
historical_period: Edo period, later reception of Sōtatsu
name_zh: 酒井抱一《风神雷神图》版本研究档

description: The great serpent in the source-scoped Kusanagi discovery account.
Named opponent in the public Smithsonian summary of the K'iche' Maya Hero Twins episode.
Guardian of the mountains of cedar confronted by Gilgameš in ETCSL 1.8.1.5.

canonical_name: Angkor Wat Churning of the Sea of Milk relief
description: In-situ bas-relief identified by APSARA in the southern section of Angkor Wat's eastern gallery.
original_name: ចម្លាក់កូរសមុទ្រទឹកដោះ

description: Principal monument of the northern group at Chichen-Itza, also known as the Temple of Kukulkan (UNESCO 483).
name_zh: 奇琴伊察卡斯蒂略（库库尔坎神庙）

description: 大英博物馆目录所载含二十一行凯布利赞歌的石碑。 / British Museum stela catalogued with a twenty-one-line hymn to Khepri.
大英博物馆登记的佛教仪式器；精确年代与产地只按馆藏页继续扩张。 / British Museum Buddhist ritual object; date and provenance remain catalogue-scoped.
historical_period: Museum-dated object; exact regional dossier requires catalogue audit

description: Ptolemaic wooden companion figure of Isis, paired with the Mourning Nephthys figure.
Ptolemaic wooden kneeling figure of Nephthys in a gesture of mourning, paired with a figure of Isis.

canonical_name: Egyptian Statue of Darius I from Susa
description: 在埃及制作、后于苏萨发现的多语铭文雕像；埃及神学与阿契美尼德王权层分别记录。 / Egyptian-made multilingual statue found at Susa; Egyptian theological and Achaemenid royal layers remain distinct.
historical_period: Achaemenid / Egyptian Dynasty 27, reign of Darius I
name_zh: 苏萨出土大流士一世埃及式雕像

canonical_name: Wind God and Thunder God Screens by Tawaraya Sotatsu
description: 建仁寺所有、京都国立博物馆官方目录记录的宗达屏风；属于后世图像层，不是古代谱系证据。 / Kennin-ji screens catalogued by Kyoto National Museum; a later visual witness, not ancient genealogy evidence.
name_zh: 俵屋宗达《风神雷神图屏风》

description: Classic Maya codex-style footed plate showing the rain god Chahk waist-deep in watery motifs.
name_zh: 大都会博物馆恰克神陶盘

canonical_name: Scarab inscribed with Amun-Re and Neit
description: 大都会艺术博物馆藏釉陶圣甲虫；底部铭刻阿蒙-拉名号。 / Met faience scarab bearing the name of Amun-Re.
name_zh: 阿蒙-拉与奈特名号圣甲虫 09.180.953

canonical_name: Roman fragments of the Great Eleusinian Relief 14.130.9
description: 大都会艺术博物馆藏十块罗马大理石摹本残片，现嵌于原作石膏模型。 / Ten Roman marble copy fragments at The Met, set into a cast of the Greek relief.
name_zh: 大厄琉息斯浮雕罗马摹本残片14.130.9

canonical_name: Book of the Dead for Nauny
description: 底比斯出土的娜乌妮葬仪纸草；目录区分《亡灵书》与冥界太阳旅程材料。 / Theban funerary papyrus whose catalogue distinguishes Book of the Dead and netherworld solar-journey material.

canonical_name: Ptah-Sokar-Osiris Figure of the Temple Musician Ihyt
description: 中空木质丧葬神像；内部材料另建 21.9.1d 档案。 / Hollow funerary figure whose catalogued contents are modeled as separate object 21.9.1d.
name_zh: 神庙乐师伊希特的卜塔-索卡尔-奥西里斯像 21.9.1a-c

description: 大都会艺术博物馆藏底比斯木质丧葬小像，来自 el-Khokha 墓 MMA 832。 / Met wooden funerary figure from el-Khokha, Tomb MMA 832.
name_zh: 帕赫伦孔苏的卜塔-索卡尔-奥西里斯像 28.3.48

description: 具有舒提冠、祈祷铭文和卡诺卜神形象的木质丧葬小像。 / Wooden funerary figure with shuty crown, prayer inscription and canopic-deity imagery.
name_zh: 佩斯乔维敏的卜塔-索卡尔-奥西里斯像 34.9

canonical_name: Linen and mud from Ptah-Sokar-Osiris figure
description: 从 21.9.1a-c 内部取出的亚麻与泥材料；与同一空腔中的麦粒和沙共同记录。 / Separately catalogued linen and mud removed from 21.9.1a-c; wheat and sand were also recorded in the cavity.
name_zh: 卜塔-索卡尔-奥西里斯像内部亚麻与泥 21.9.1d

description: 大都会艺术博物馆藏拉-哈拉赫提釉陶护符。 / Met faience amulet catalogued as Ra Horakhty.

canonical_name: Stela with man offering to Re-Harakhty
description: 库施时期木碑，描绘人物向拉-哈拉赫提献香。 / Kushite-era wooden stela showing an offering to Re-Harakhty.
name_zh: 向拉-哈拉赫提献祭未完成木碑 O.C.81

canonical_name: Vajra with Angry Heads and Makara Prongs 1994.605.43
description: 大都会馆藏的唐代鎏金青铜仪式器；不是《梨俱吠陀》叙事中的那一件武器。 / Tang-dynasty gilt-bronze ritual object, not the mythic weapon-token in Rigveda 1.32.
original_name: 唐 鎏金青銅金剛杵

description: 厄琉息斯出土的大型浮雕，博物馆目录识别得墨忒耳、珀耳塞福涅与特里普托勒摩斯。 / Monumental relief from Eleusis catalogued with Demeter, Persephone and Triptolemos.

雅典国家考古博物馆的陶制奉献板；登记馆藏、奉献语境与图像解释边界，不把图像当作秘仪全程记录。 / Clay votive tablet in the National Archaeological Museum; custody and dedication are registered without treating its imagery as a complete ritual record.
historical_period: Classical Greek, about fourth century BCE

name_zh: 雷神锤环形护符藏品组

description: 鲁宾馆藏西藏金属仪式权杖；其“方法”象征属于馆藏解释层。 / Eighteenth-century Tibetan ritual scepter; symbolism remains museum interpretation.

canonical_name: Wind God and Thunder God Screens by Ogata Kōrin A-11189-1
description: 东京国立博物馆重要文化财产；与宗达原作保持为两件不同对象。 / Tokyo National Museum Important Cultural Property; a distinct object from Sōtatsu’s earlier screens.
name_zh: 尾形光琳《风神雷神图屏风》A-11189-1

description: Retainer of King Kang of Song whose wife is taken by the king; husband and wife both die rather than be parted, and catalpa trees joined above their separate graves are called the trees of longing (Soushen ji, juan 11).
Young man of Nanyang who meets a ghost by night, pretends to be a new ghost, learns that ghosts fear human spittle, and sells the ghost as a sheep in the market of Wan (Soushen ji, juan 16).
Younger sister of the queen Neferure and daughter of the prince of Bakhtan, possessed by a spirit and healed by the god Khonsu-the-Provider in the Bentresh Stela.
Father of Kullervo, thought slain by his brother Untamo but found living with his family at the edge of Lapland (Kalevala, Runes XXXI, XXXIV–XXXVI).
Blind old herdsman of Pohjola scorned by Lemminkäinen, who waits at the river of Tuonela and kills him with a water-serpent (Kalevala, Runes XII, XIV).

Brother of Kalervo who, after a run of petty quarrels, destroys Kalervo's people, fails three times to kill the infant Kullervo and sells him to Ilmarinen; his clan is later wiped out by Kullervo (Kalevala, Runes XXXI, XXXVI).
Most arrogant of Penelope's suitors, who plots to ambush Telemachus and is the first to die when Odysseus strings his bow (Odyssey 1–22).
Loyal swineherd of Odysseus, a king's son kidnapped in childhood, who shelters his disguised master and fights beside him against the suitors (Odyssey 14–22).
Old nurse of Odysseus who recognises him by the boar-tusk scar on his thigh as she washes his feet (Odyssey 19).

Athenian who received Dionysus and learned from him to make wine; shepherds who drank it unmixed thought themselves poisoned and killed him, and his daughter Erigone hanged herself in grief (Apollodorus, Library 3.14.7).

Son of Dryas, king of the Edonians in Thrace, who insulted and expelled Dionysus; driven mad, he killed his own son, and his people had him torn apart by horses on Mount Pangaeum (Apollodorus, Library 3.5.1).
name_zh: 吕枯耳戈斯（厄多涅斯人的国王）

description: King of Seriphos who sends Perseus for the Gorgon's head and is turned to stone by it (Library 2.4.2–2.4.3).
Childless king of Madra who after eighteen years of offerings is granted a daughter, Sāvitrī, by the goddess Sāvitrī (Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Pativratā-māhātmya).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Blind king of Śālva driven from his throne, who lives in a forest hermitage with his son Satyavān; Sāvitrī's boons restore his sight and his kingdom (Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Pativratā-māhātmya).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Brother of Nala who, aided by Kali, wins Nala's kingdom at dice and loses it back to him when Nala returns with the science of dice (Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Nalopākhyāna).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: King of Ayodhyā who takes Nala as his charioteer Bāhuka, drives with him to Damayantī's second svayaṃvara and teaches him the science of dice in exchange for the science of horses (Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Nalopākhyāna).
historical_period: Mahābhārata (Sanskrit epic, composed c. 4th century BCE – 4th century CE)

description: Bravo of Izumo whom Yamato Takeru befriends, tricks into exchanging his sword for a wooden one while bathing in the Hi river, and kills (Kojiki, Sect. LXXXI).
Twelfth sovereign in the Kojiki's sequence, ruling from the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku, who sends his fierce son Yamato Takeru first west and then east (Kojiki, Sect. LXXVI–XC).
original_name: 大帶日子淤斯呂和氣天皇

description: Two brothers, the bravoes of Kumaso in the west, killed at their housewarming feast by Yamato Takeru disguised as a girl; the younger gives him the name Yamato Takeru as he dies (Kojiki, Sect. LXXX).
古诺斯人类起源叙事中的男性人物，按具体文本见证建档。 / Male figure in Old Norse human-origin narratives, recorded at witness level.
古诺斯人类起源叙事中的女性人物，按具体文本见证建档。 / Female figure in Old Norse human-origin narratives, recorded at witness level.
King of Tūrān and enemy of Iran, who arms Sohrāb against Iran and charges his generals to keep father and son from knowing each other (Shahnameh).

Rash shah of Iran who, lured by a demon minstrel, invades Māzandarān and is blinded and captured by the White Demon until Rostam frees him; he later tries to fly to heaven on an eagle-drawn throne (Shahnameh).
Shah of Iran who receives the young Zāl, has his wise men test him with riddles, and consents to his marriage (Shahnameh).
King of Kābul descended from the tyrant Zahhāk, father of Rūdābeh and husband of Sindokht (Shahnameh).
Local lord of Māzandarān captured by Rostam in the fifth stage, who guides him to the White Demon and is afterwards made ruler of Māzandarān (Shahnameh).

科塔尔为巴力制作的第二件有名武器；外形译法不一。 / Second named weapon made for Baal by Kothar; translated object form varies.
